steps.name: prompt
steps.text: Write the introduction for our paper on VERVE, a system that rewrites counselor-in-training responses into better reflections for Motivational Interviewing. It should motivate the problem, define the rewriting task, and summarize the approach and results.

steps.name: skeleton_outline
steps.text:
- Rising mental health need during Covid-19
- Counselor shortage, slow training, NLP efforts so far
- Gap: no "mentoring" tools -> task of counselor response rewriting
- Figure 1 example: why scores / reference reflections are not enough
- VERVE: template editing, two techniques, evaluation

steps.name: detailed_outline
steps.text:
Rising need
- Covid-19: people living with anxiety and depression rose more than four times
- worsens disparity: unmet need for mental health treatment vs. increased disorders

Counselor shortage / training
- shortage of mental health professionals; becoming a counselor = extensive training
- training hard to speed up: expert supervision; laborious, time-extensive evaluative feedback
- NLP for counselor training: automatic coding of counselor behavior; timing + language suggestions during client interactions; evaluating quality of specific counseling skills

Gap and new task
- limited progress on tools in a "mentoring role" giving alternative language suggestions to trainees
- new task: counselor response rewriting = rephrase trainee responses with basic skills into responses with more advanced proficiency
- skill: reflective listening; strategy: Motivational Interviewing

Example (Figure 1)
- numerical score or reference reflection (high-quality reflection) doesn't tell counselor what to improve
- our system: separate behavior-relevant (reflection-like language) from behavior-non-relevant parts
- non-relevant parts used as template for improved rewrite

VERVE
- name: Reflecti VE R ewriting for Moti V ational Int E rviewing
- based on template editing from text style transfer; no parallel data (expert annotation of rewrites expensive, time-consuming)
- paraphrase-augmented training: flexible mapping masked template -> full response; rewrite structure not constrained by template
- adaptive template updating: content-edit trade-off (keep part of user response vs. full rewrite); iteratively update masked template based on effect of rewrite
- automatic evaluation vs. text style transfer baselines: higher reflection scores, content preserved

steps.name: partial_draft
steps.text:
During the Covid-19 pandemic the number of people living with anxiety and depression went up more than four times. This made the existing disparity worse, between the unmet need for mental health treatment and the increase in mental health disorders.

One reason for this gap is that there are not enough mental health professionals, and this is made worse because becoming a counselor takes extensive training. Counselor training is hard to speed up for several reasons, for example it needs expert supervision, and giving evaluative feedback is a laborious process that takes a lot of time. There have been some efforts to use NLP to help with counselor training. These include automatic coding of counselor behavior, giving timing and language suggestions while the counselor is interacting with clients, and evaluating the quality of specific counseling skills.

But progress on tools that can take a "mentoring role" and suggest alternative language for counselors in training has been limited. To address this, we introduce a new task called counselor response rewriting. In this task, trainee responses that use basic counseling skills are rephrased into alternative responses that show a more advanced level of counseling proficiency. The counseling skill we focus on is reflective listening, and the counseling strategy is Motivational Interviewing.

Example (Figure 1)
- numerical score or reference reflection (high-quality reflection) doesn't tell counselor what to improve
- our system: separate behavior-relevant (reflection-like language) from behavior-non-relevant parts
- non-relevant parts used as template for improved rewrite

VERVE
- name: Reflecti VE R ewriting for Moti V ational Int E rviewing
- based on template editing from text style transfer; no parallel data (expert annotation of rewrites expensive, time-consuming)
- paraphrase-augmented training: flexible mapping masked template -> full response; rewrite structure not constrained by template
- adaptive template updating: content-edit trade-off (keep part of user response vs. full rewrite); iteratively update masked template based on effect of rewrite
- automatic evaluation vs. text style transfer baselines: higher reflection scores, content preserved

steps.name: rough_draft
steps.text:
During the Covid-19 pandemic the number of people living with anxiety and depression went up more than four times. This made the existing disparity worse, between the unmet need for mental health treatment and the increase in mental health disorders.

One reason for this gap is that there are not enough mental health professionals, and this is made worse because becoming a counselor takes extensive training. Counselor training is hard to speed up for several reasons, for example it needs expert supervision, and giving evaluative feedback is a laborious process that takes a lot of time. There have been some efforts to use NLP to help with counselor training. These include automatic coding of counselor behavior, giving timing and language suggestions while the counselor is interacting with clients, and evaluating the quality of specific counseling skills.

But progress on tools that can take a "mentoring role" and suggest alternative language for counselors in training has been limited. To address this, we introduce a new task called counselor response rewriting. In this task, trainee responses that use basic counseling skills are rephrased into alternative responses that show a more advanced level of counseling proficiency. The counseling skill we focus on is reflective listening, and the counseling strategy is Motivational Interviewing.

Figure 1 shows an example of what our system outputs. In this case, giving the counselor a numerical score or a reference reflection (that is, a high-quality reflection) does not help them understand which parts of their answer could be better. Our system deals with this problem. It separates the parts that are relevant to the behavior (for example reflection-like language) from the parts that are not relevant, and then it uses the non-relevant parts as a template to create an improved rewrite of the original.

We introduce VERVE (Reflecti VE R ewriting for Moti V ational Int E rviewing). VERVE is a framework based on template editing methods from text style transfer, and these methods do not need parallel data, which is important because expert annotation of rewritten responses is expensive and takes a lot of time. We propose two simple techniques to adapt template-based text rewriting to counseling: paraphrase-augmented training and adaptive template updating. Paraphrase-augmented training helps the text generator learn a more flexible mapping from a masked template to a full response, so the structure of the final rewrite is not constrained by the template. Adaptive template updating handles the content-edit trade-off (for example keeping part of the user response instead of rewriting all of it) by updating the masked template iteratively based on the effect of the rewrite. We compare our framework with several baselines from earlier text style transfer work using automatic evaluation, and our system gets higher reflection scores than the baselines while it still preserves content from the original response.

steps.name: revised_draft
steps.text:
During the Covid-19 pandemic, the number of people living with anxiety and depression rose more than four times, aggravating the existing disparity between unmet needs for mental health treatment and increased mental health disorders [1].

One driving cause behind this discrepancy is the shortage of mental health professionals, which is made worse by the fact that becoming a counselor requires extensive training [2]. In particular, counselor training is difficult to speed up because of several factors, such as the need for expert supervision and the laborious, time-extensive process needed to provide evaluative feedback. There have been several efforts to use NLP to assist counselor training, including automatic coding of counselor behavior [3], providing timing and language suggestions during client interactions [4,5], and evaluating the quality of specific counseling skills [6,7].

However, progress in developing tools that can fulfill a "mentoring role" and offer alternative language suggestions for counselors in training has been limited. To fill this gap, we introduce the task of counselor response rewriting, which involves rephrasing trainees' responses with basic counseling skills into alternative responses that reflect a more advanced level of counseling proficiency. We focus on reflective listening as our main counseling skill, and on Motivational Interviewing [8] as the counseling strategy.

We show an example of our system output in Figure 1. Here, providing a numerical score or a reference reflection (i.e., a high-quality reflection) does not help the counselor understand which parts of their answer could be improved. Our system addresses this by separating the behavior-relevant parts (e.g., reflection-like language) from the behavior-non-relevant parts, and using the latter as a template for creating an improved rewrite of the original.

We introduce VERVE (Reflecti VE R ewriting for Moti V ational Int E rviewing), a framework based on template editing methods from text style transfer that do not require parallel data, since expert annotation of rewritten responses is expensive and time-consuming. We propose two simple techniques to adapt template-based text rewriting to the counseling domain: paraphrase-augmented training and adaptive template updating. The first helps the text generator learn a more flexible mapping between a masked template and a full response, so that the structure of the final rewrite is not constrained by the template. The second handles the content-edit trade-off (e.g., preserving part of the user response rather than rewriting it completely) by iteratively updating the masked template based on the effect of the rewrite. We evaluate our framework against several baselines from previous text style transfer work using automatic evaluation and show that our system outperforms the baselines in achieved reflection scores while still preserving content from the original response.
